rules.intro: On the typed path a card's rules text is read once, when its card is first loaded, and the parse is kept. From then on the engine works on typed data: ability hosts holding instructions in printed order, each carried to resolution by the one carrier its trigger event names, performed by the one executor its verb has, through the one module that owns the rule. Whatever a step cannot type or run is refused and stays on its legacy path, recorded rather than guessed. The legacy paths that still read text at runtime are counted by ratchets that may only fall.

stages.title: Printed text
stages.body: MTGJSON oracle text for every Modern-legal card, loaded from the ModernAtomic parts with their provenance. Reminder text is stripped and the card's own name masked before the grammar reads the text.

stages.title: Clause grammar
stages.body: Six layers, once per face: L0 normalises with an offset map, L1 cuts paragraphs into ability hosts, L2–L3 frame sentences and split clauses, L4 types each clause through the verb lexicon and nine closed sub-grammars, L5 links references ("them", "that card") and branches. A clause it cannot type becomes UNMODELLED, with the stage that stopped it.

stages.title: Typed hosts
stages.body: Frozen, hashable data: per face a tuple of hosts — spell, mode, activated, loyalty, triggered, static, keyword — each with its trigger head, costs, targets and instructions. Instructions carry an actor, a filter, an amount, a destination and a condition, plus "if you do", "otherwise" and "instead" branches.

stages.title: Carriers
stages.body: Where a game event meets a host: entering, attacking, a cast, the beginning of a step, a draw, combat damage, an activation, a loyalty line, a spell resolving. A carrier takes a card's hosts whole or not at all. A modal trigger's modes and every target are chosen as it is put on the stack (CR 603.3c–d).

stages.title: Strict views and the gate
stages.body: Each family declares the exact shapes it runs. can_execute fails closed: every instruction needs an executor whose supports admits its shape, an evaluator for each condition, a supported entry for each filter key, and a reference that names the instruction whose result it binds.

stages.title: Dispatcher and executors
stages.body: The dispatcher owns sequencing (CR 608.2c): printed order, conditions, optional effects asked of their controller, "instead" replacements, delayed and reflexive sub-abilities. Each instruction is one executor call (engine/effect_executors.py). An executor never reads text, never picks a target and never scores.

stages.title: Owners
stages.body: Targets go through engine/target_solver.py, damage and life through engine/damage.py, zone moves through the zone funnel, land entry through engine/land_manager.py, "unless" costs through engine/optional_costs.py, counters through CardInstance.add_plus_counters. A CI ratchet counts every second path.

auditor.title: The auditor watches every stage
auditor.body: Opt-in and observation-only: with MTG_RULES_AUDIT unset every game is byte-identical. Each invariant restates a rule from the raw fields, independently of the code it checks, and records a violation with seed, decks and turn. Census rows count what no carrier took yet, so a matrix run ranks what to build next.

trace.why: One host, two carriers: the enter and the attack carrier both take it. The search finds what its description admits, the searcher chooses (the AI by its one land valuation), and the land-entry owner puts the lands onto the battlefield tapped.

An exile that lasts until the enchantment leaves (CR 610.3), energy given as player counters (CR 122.1), and a beginning-of-step sacrifice that its controller avoids by paying an "unless" cost (CR 118.12).

A modal attack trigger: its controller chooses the mode as it is put on the stack, and each mode runs as a host of its own (CR 603.3c, 700.2). Its domain power is still read by the legacy characteristic-defining parser.
A spell whose second sentence replaces its first under a condition: the dispatcher runs the "instead" instruction at its victim's place when delirium holds.
Fail closed. The attack host's "you may pay {E}{E}{E}" has no executor yet, so the attack carrier refuses the card and its legacy path runs. It is one of the census rows still open.

boundary.intro: The engine enumerates the legal options and never scores them; the AI chooses and never changes game state. Every choice crosses one typed seam, the callbacks protocol. A choice the AI has no opinion on falls back to an engine default built from printed data alone, so a game with no AI attached still plays legally.

guards.intro: Each change is a unit: one rule, fixed for every card it covers. Before it lands it has to pass these checks, and none of them can be argued with in review.

protocol.title: Symptom, then rule
protocol.body: A replay, an audit row or a census row names a card. The unit names the Comprehensive Rules sentence the engine broke, with its CR number. If the rule cannot be written without a card name, it isn't understood yet.

protocol.title: Size the class
protocol.body: tools/class_census.py counts the pool cards the rule covers. Ten or more is a mechanic. Fewer is widened to its CR family, or recorded as a gap and not built.

protocol.title: One owner
protocol.body: One module owns each rule. An existing field or primitive is reused before anything is written, since a second implementation of an existing rule is the most common defect.

protocol.title: Typed at load
protocol.body: The rule's card knowledge is parsed once into typed data. No runtime oracle reads, no name keys, and a name-keyed handler the class covers is deleted in the same commit.

protocol.title: Red test first
protocol.body: The test is named for the rule, not a card, and is seen failing before the fix lands with it. The rules auditor gets an independent invariant, tested both ways.

protocol.title: Prove every difference
protocol.body: The host harness runs each switched host against its legacy path on six boards and two seeds. Every pair that differs needs a written reason. The seeded digest and the win-rate anchor replay any game that changes, and only rules-correct play is accepted.

protocol.title: Measure, pinned
protocol.body: Both test halves run from a worktree pinned at the commit. A same-seed best-of-three matrix arm runs on Actions with the LLM scorer offline. The tracker records the rule, the class size, the commits, the measurement and the leads not built.

pipeline.title: Board snapshot
pipeline.body: The board is captured as an EVSnapshot (ai/ev_evaluator.py): life, power, mana, storm count, energy, evasive and lifelink power, cards in hand. It is cheap to copy and project, so every candidate play is scored on a projected snapshot.
pipeline.formula: EVSnapshot { my_life: 17, opp_life: 14, my_power: 6, my_clock: 3, opp_clock: 5 }

pipeline.title: Game plan phase
pipeline.body: GoalEngine (ai/gameplan.py) reads each deck's goal sequence from decks/gameplans/*.json and tracks where the deck is in it. Card priorities and roles come from that file, never from Python source.

pipeline.title: Score every legal play
pipeline.body: Every legal action is scored in one currency: position value from the clock (ai/clock.py), turns to kill minus turns to die. A burn spell and a creature compete on one scale. A CI ratchet refuses any new bare number in ai/: each constant is named and justified in ai/scoring_constants.py.

pipeline.title: Bayesian hand inference
pipeline.body: ai/bhi.py tracks the opponent's chance of holding a counter, removal or burn, updated on priority passes, spells cast and open mana. All of it is read from card tags, never card names.
pipeline.formula: P(counter | pass) = P(pass | counter) · P(counter) / P(pass)

pipeline.title: Plan the turn
pipeline.body: ai/turn_planner.py orders the same plays several ways (deploy then attack, remove then attack, attack then deploy, hold mana, lethal push) on a virtual board. Blocks are predicted jointly, and first strike resolves in two steps.

pipeline.title: Execute and log
pipeline.body: The best play is executed through the engine. Its candidates, scores and reasons go to the strategic log, which the replay viewer prints beside each play.

layers.title: Card data and deck knowledge
layers.body: Every card in the Modern pool from MTGJSON, merged from provenance-checked parts. Decklists, meta shares and per-deck gameplans are data files. No engine or AI conditional names a card or a deck.
